# Glossary {#sec-glossary .unnumbered}

This glossary defines key terms used throughout *Physical AI*. Terms are organized alphabetically.

```{=latex}
\small\sloppy
\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\setlist[description]{
  style=unboxed,

## A {#sec-glossary-vol4-a .unlisted}

**Action Chunking**
: A policy technique in which a model predicts a sequence of future actions rather than one action per inference. Executing part of a chunk amortizes inference latency but leaves that interval open loop with respect to new policy observations. Receding-horizon replanning or temporal ensembling can improve responsiveness and continuity; neither chunking nor blending establishes kinematic feasibility or collision clearance. (@Sec-brain, @sec-planning, @sec-training)

**Administrative Lease ($T_{\text{admin}}$)**
: The bound, inside an intent lease, on how long the application processor may hold a goal without renewing it. It caps the harm a hung or crashed host can do while its last goal stays active; it is one of the three deadlines whose earliest sets the intent lease's expiry. (@Sec-intent)

## B {#sec-glossary-vol4-b .unlisted}

**Behavioral Cloning (BC)**
: The foundational imitation learning paradigm that trains a policy via supervised learning to directly map sensory observations to expert control actions, treating physical sequential decision-making as a direct regression or classification task. While computationally efficient on static demonstration archives, standard behavioral cloning ignores the closed-loop consequences of its own control outputs. Small single-step errors can therefore move the robot away from the demonstration distribution, where later errors may compound without learned recovery behavior. (@Sec-training, @sec-data)

**Belief State Invalidation Horizon ($T_{\text{inv}}$)**
: The elapsed temporal duration beyond which an unobserved spatial or kinematic state estimate can no longer be certified to lie within a task's safe tolerance envelope. Derived from disturbance and motion bounds or a declared probabilistic uncertainty model, it limits how long perceptual memory supports the claim. A covariance-based horizon retains the confidence assumptions of that model. Downstream planners that treat spatial beliefs older than this horizon as valid free space risk commanding collisions with dynamic obstacles. (@Sec-memory, @sec-appendix-control-covariance)

**Bumpless Transfer**
: A dynamic control handoff protocol that matches controller state and commanded references across control authorities to avoid abrupt changes in actuator effort. When supervisory control transitions abruptly between an autonomous neural policy and a human operator, unmatched commands can induce mechanical shocks, structural oscillations, or loss of traction. Bumpless transfer employs dynamic transition ramps and feedback state tracking to transfer command authority smoothly; effort and slew limits still require separate checks. (@Sec-intervention, @sec-appendix-control-splines)

## C {#sec-glossary-vol4-c .unlisted}

**Causal Boundary**
: The physical, energetic, and architectural threshold in an embodied system where reversible digital computations terminate and irreversible physical work is performed on the external environment ($dW = \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{x}$). Beyond this boundary, computational errors cannot be rolled back by software exception handlers or abort routines, requiring a qualified permission check before actuation under the declared safety assumptions. The permission path sits above this boundary, at the proposal boundary of @sec-boundary-machine-model. (@Sec-boundary, @sec-body)

**Causal Confusion (Causal Misidentification)**
: An imitation learning failure mode where a policy conditions on spurious, non-causal features that correlate with expert actions in training demonstrations rather than the true physical affordances of the task. High-capacity neural models exploit incidental visual cues (such as interface indicators, dashboard lights, or past actions) that disappear or change under physical deployment. When deployment breaks these correlations, the policy can select inappropriate actions even if its demonstration loss was low. (@Sec-training)

**Chunk Lease ($T_{\text{lease}}$)**
: The execution lease of the autonomous chunk policy, which bounds how long an admitted chunk may keep driving the actuators before a renewal must arrive. It is chosen, then checked against the ceiling the stopping budget derives, and it enters the total pre-brake delay because a stalled proposer is noticed only when its lease expires. (@Sec-nervous, @sec-enforcement)

**Clearance Inset Margin**
: A geometric buffer subtracted from estimated free space to account for perception, calibration, transform, information-age, and tracking uncertainty. Deterministic error bounds can support a worst-case inset; covariance instead requires a stated distribution and confidence level and does not supply an absolute bound. The clearance claim holds only while the combined uncertainty model and its operating assumptions remain valid. (@Sec-perception, @sec-planning)

**Closed-Loop Evaluation**
: The metrological paradigm in physical AI that measures a policy's performance, safety, and stability through interactive rollouts on physical hardware or high-fidelity simulation, rather than through static loss metrics on a held-out dataset. Because an autonomous policy continuously perturbs its own operating environment, meaningful evaluation requires logging closed-loop metrics such as task completion rates, dynamic safety margin violations, and mean operational time between interventions. Open-loop validation error alone does not measure the consequences of policy-induced distribution shift. (@Sec-evaluation, @sec-training)

**Compounding Rollout Error**
: The accumulation of task error when a policy's actions move it into states poorly represented in expert demonstrations. Under standard finite-horizon imitation-learning assumptions, a per-step expert-distribution error rate $\epsilon$ can yield worst-case excess accumulated task cost of order $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon T^2)$ over horizon $T$. This is not a universal law for physical displacement, tracking error, or collision probability. (@Sec-training, @sec-appendix-ml-compounding)

**Control Barrier Function (CBF)**
: A continuously differentiable function $h(\mathbf{x})$ defining a candidate safe set $\mathcal{C}=\{\mathbf{x}:h(\mathbf{x})\ge 0\}$. Under the required dynamics and regularity assumptions, enforcing $\dot h\ge-\alpha(h)$ with feasible controls and a suitable increasing function $\alpha$ satisfying $\alpha(0)=0$ can establish forward invariance from an initial state in $\mathcal{C}$; for control-affine dynamics, this condition is affine in the input and can constrain a quadratic-program safety filter. Physical implementation also requires qualified state and model error bounds, actuator limits, and sampled-data timing; the continuous-time condition alone does not establish those premises. (@Sec-enforcement, @sec-appendix-control-cbf)

**Cross-Embodiment Transfer**
: A learning paradigm in which a single policy or foundation model is trained on sensorimotor data gathered across heterogeneous robot morphologies, kinematic chains, and actuator dynamics to generalize to novel target embodiments. Achieving cross-embodiment generalization requires accounting for differences in observations, action semantics, and body dynamics, for example through shared representations or embodiment-specific adapters. Its primary challenge is preventing negative transfer induced by unmodeled dynamic discrepancies, link inertia variations, and differing joint velocity boundaries. (@Sec-data, @sec-training)

## D {#sec-glossary-vol4-d .unlisted}

**Diffusion Policy**
: A generative policy that produces continuous action sequences by iteratively denoising a noisy candidate conditioned on observations. It can represent multiple demonstration modes without forcing their average, but generated chunks still require feasibility and clearance checks. The number and cost of denoising steps contribute to inference latency. (@Sec-training, @sec-appendix-ml-diffusion)

**Domain Randomization (DR)**
: A sim-to-real transfer methodology that systematically perturbs physical parameters (mass, friction, damping, motor torque limits), sensor characteristics (noise covariance, latency, camera pose), and visual textures across simulated training episodes. By exposing the policy to a broad distribution of simulated environments, domain randomization encourages the neural network to learn invariant representations and feedback behaviors robust to the chosen variation; transfer still depends on whether that variation covers the relevant physical conditions. If randomized too narrowly, the real world falls outside the training hull; if randomized too broadly, learning can become harder or the resulting behavior overly conservative. (@Sec-training)

**Dynamic Stopping Distance ($d_{\text{stop}}$)**
: The clearance needed to stop from the current state, including pre-brake delay, the selected braking trajectory, and localization and protective allowances. With constant speed $v$ during delay and constant braking deceleration $a_{\text{brake}}>0$, the model is $d_{\text{stop}}=v\tau_{\text{delay}}+v^2/(2a_{\text{brake}})+\delta_{\text{loc}}+\delta_{\text{margin}}$. A ramped or jerk-limited stop requires its own profile integral; the permission path must reserve that distance together with the tracking inset and any remaining timing margin. (@Sec-body, @sec-enforcement)

## E {#sec-glossary-vol4-e .unlisted}

**Endogenous Covariate Shift**
: A distribution shift in sequential decision-making where an embodied agent's own execution errors drive its physical body into states unrepresented in its training demonstrations, thereby presenting the policy with novel out-of-distribution observations. An offline action-loss objective does not itself constrain the states visited by the deployed policy, so errors can compound along the trajectory. In physical systems, this shift can cause task failure or boundary violations; corrective data and feedback can improve recovery but require evaluation in the affected states. (@Sec-boundary, @sec-data, @sec-training)

**Endogenous Experience (The Action–Observation Loop)**
: The closed-loop data generation process wherein an agent's executed actions causally determine its subsequent physical states and sensory observations ($s_{t+1} \sim P(s \mid s_t, a_t)$). Unlike passive supervised learning on fixed, exogenous datasets, physical AI experience generation forms an irreversible dynamical feedback loop where minor control perturbations alter future data collection trajectories. Consequently, data generation and policy deployment are fundamentally inseparable in embodied agents. (@Sec-boundary, @sec-data)

**Envelope Trichotomy**
: A three-valued epistemic classification of cyber-physical runtime health that partitions system status relative to its certified operating envelope into *known-true* (verified valid telemetry inside bounds), *known-false* (verified limit breach), and *unknown* (epistemic uncertainty from sensor corruption, frame drops, or estimator divergence). In embodied AI, both *known-false* and *unknown* withhold tracking permission and select the qualified fallback for the current state and surviving hardware. (@Sec-release)

**Execution Lease**
: Authority an admitted command source holds to keep driving the actuators without renewal. It begins at admission, not at dispatch, and its expiry invokes the state-matched fallback rather than the next proposal. The chunk lease and the manual lease are its two instances on the running machine. (@Sec-nervous, @sec-enforcement, @sec-intervention)

**Exposure Wall**
: The limit on what failure-free operation alone can establish about a rare failure rate. Under a stationary Poisson failure model, bounding a catastrophic rate $\lambda = 10^{-9}$ per hour at 95 percent confidence requires about $-\ln(0.05)/\lambda \approx 3.0 \times 10^9$ failure-free hours of exposure from the same configuration, an argument Butler and Finelli made for flight software. The required exposure makes direct demonstration impractical, so claims at that level also need architectural evidence, fault injection, and justified operating premises. (@Sec-evaluation-trial-limits, @sec-verification, @sec-appendix-ml-exposure)

## F {#sec-glossary-vol4-f .unlisted}

**Fallback Ladder**
: The ordered set of responses the permission path selects when a proposal cannot be admitted unchanged or its premises fail. Its rungs are PROJECT (minimal-intervention projection of the proposal onto the safe set), HOLD (a state-matched powered hold), STOP (a controlled, state-matched stop), and INHIBIT (drive torque inhibit with a separately rated brake). Each response requires a validated entry region and surviving hardware; selection must occur while that response remains feasible. An invalid replacement need not revoke an active trajectory whose own premises still hold. (@Sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder, @sec-intervention)

**Flow Matching Policy**
: A generative policy trained to predict a vector field that transports samples from a base distribution toward a conditional action distribution. The training probability path and sample coupling determine the transport construction; straight conditional paths do not imply globally optimal transport or straight learned sample trajectories. Sampling cost depends on the trained field, numerical solver, and required accuracy, so fewer inference steps than diffusion must be demonstrated for the selected policies. (@Sec-training)

**Forward Invariance**
: A property of a dynamical system, control policy, and set $\mathcal{C}$: every trajectory starting in $\mathcal{C}$ remains in $\mathcal{C}$ for all future time under the stated assumptions. A barrier certificate can establish this property for a modeled system with feasible controls. Applying the result to hardware requires maintaining the state, disturbance, actuation, and timing premises of the certificate. (@Sec-enforcement, @sec-appendix-control-cbf)

## G {#sec-glossary-vol4-g .unlisted}

**Grounded Affordance**
: The spatial, kinematic, and dynamic interaction manifold associated with an object or terrain region that defines where and how an embodied agent can initiate, sustain, and complete a physical manipulation or locomotion primitive. Unlike purely semantic object labels, a grounded affordance parameterizes contact surface normals, friction cone bounds, end-effector approach corridors, and kinematically feasible grasp poses relative to the robot's physical embodiment. A semantic task request cannot be translated into physical action until its underlying affordance is rigorously grounded within the robot's reachable workspace. (@Sec-intent, @sec-perception)

## H {#sec-glossary-vol4-h .unlisted}

**Heterogeneous Silicon Partitioning**
: Allocation of learned workloads and time-critical permission or control loops to different compute resources, with hardware protection of memory and peripheral access. Separate processors and dedicated buses can remove specific interference and fault paths, but shared power, clocks, interconnects, or thermal limits can retain common-mode failures. Timing and fault-containment claims therefore require evidence for the actual partition and declared load and fault envelope. (@Sec-placement, @sec-appendix-systems-ipc)

**Hardware Lease**
: A countdown timer on the safety microcontroller that enforces a lease's expiry without the cooperation of the process that issued the authority. It is the mechanism behind every other lease, since a hung host cannot extend authority that a hardware timer is counting down. (@Sec-intent, @sec-enforcement)

## I {#sec-glossary-vol4-i .unlisted}

**Inevitable Collision State (ICS)**
: A physical system state $\mathbf{x}(t)$ from which no admissible, physically executable control trajectory exists—within dynamic actuator and friction limits—that can prevent impact with environmental obstacles over an infinite time horizon. Unlike geometric obstacle clearance, an ICS explicitly accounts for plant momentum, friction limits, dynamic obstacle trajectories, and finite actuator braking authority. A machine can enter an ICS before contact; insufficient stopping distance establishes this only when no other admissible evasive trajectory avoids impact. (@Sec-body, @sec-planning, @sec-enforcement)

**Intent Grounding Refusal**
: A deterministic safety rejection mechanism whereby an intent translation engine or admittance gate formally refuses to execute a high-level command because the requested goal cannot be physically or safely grounded. Refusal is triggered when semantic targets lack reachable affordance manifolds, demand trajectories that violate kinodynamic feasibility, or conflict with verified safety invariants. Rather than silently attempting an unreachable or hazardous motion, the system emits an explicit refusal diagnostic, signaling supervisory intervention or deliberative replanning. (@Sec-intent, @sec-intervention)

**Intent Lease**
: The record, eighth in the record chain, that turns a grounded human goal into a bounded, expiring request that grants a target, a tolerance, and effort ceilings, but never a path. It expires at the earliest of its evidence horizon, its administrative lease, and its stopping deadline, and expiry withdraws the authority based on that intent and requires re-grounding or a qualified state-matched fallback. Unlike an execution lease, it bounds which trajectories may be admitted, not how long an admitted command may run. (@Sec-intent, @sec-planning)

**Intervention Masking**
: An empirical evaluation and safety pathology where repeated, proactive interventions by human supervisors systematically distort autonomy metrics by intercepting the policy before it encounters critical boundary failures. Because the supervisor intervenes during nascent drift, assisted success and accident counts alone do not reveal how the unaided policy would have behaved after takeover. Logs must distinguish intervention classes, exposure, and task outcomes. Reporting these separately prevents assisted task completion from being mistaken for evidence of independent policy competence. (@Sec-intervention, @sec-evaluation)

**Intervention Rate**
: The number of events in a declared intervention class divided by active operating time, or by distance when a distance-based rate is reported. The rate depends on the intervention policy and exposure population; human takeovers and automatic corrections must remain distinguishable. It does not by itself establish safety or stability. (@Sec-evaluation, @sec-intervention)

## K {#sec-glossary-vol4-k .unlisted}

**Kinodynamic Feasibility**
: The mathematical property of a planned physical trajectory that simultaneously satisfies geometric configuration-space collision avoidance constraints, kinematic mechanism limits (joint positions and velocities), and dynamic plant boundaries (actuator torques, joint accelerations, reflected jerk, and contact friction cones). A purely kinematic trajectory can exceed actuator torque-speed or tire adhesion limits, causing saturation and tracking error. Trajectory synthesis in physical AI requires verifying kinodynamic feasibility across the entire motion horizon prior to execution. (@Sec-planning, @sec-body)

## M {#sec-glossary-vol4-m .unlisted}

**Manual Lease ($T_{\text{lease,man}}$)**
: The execution lease of a human operator in manual mode, renewed by authenticated heartbeats. It replaces the chunk lease in the total pre-brake delay while the operator drives, so it must fit the stopping reserve of the mode in which it is granted. (@Sec-intervention)

**Mean Time Between Interventions (MTBI)**
: Active operating time divided by the number of events in a declared intervention class. MTBI is the reciprocal of the time-based intervention rate when the count is nonzero; a zero-event run requires an exposure-based statistical bound rather than a claim of infinite reliability. Interrupted trials and the intervention policy affect interpretation, so MTBI alone does not establish safety or stability. (@Sec-evaluation, @sec-intervention)

**Metric 3D Lifting (Spatial Grounding)**
: The construction of a three-dimensional scene representation in physical units and a declared coordinate frame from sensor observations. Metric scale requires calibrated geometry, depth measurements, or another validated scale reference; image features and reconstruction methods alone do not resolve monocular scale ambiguity. The representation supports reachability and collision checks only within its uncertainty, coverage, and information-age bounds. (@Sec-perception, @sec-intent)

**Minimal Risk Maneuver (MRM)**
: A fallback maneuver intended to reduce risk after a fault or loss of nominal authority, such as a controlled stop or transition to a supported resting configuration. Its feasibility depends on the current state, available clearance, and surviving sensing, actuation, and power. The designation does not guarantee a hazard-free outcome or require every machine to reach an immediate standstill. (@Sec-enforcement, @sec-intervention)

**Minimal-Intervention Safety Shield**
: A supervisory filter that modifies a nominal control proposal only as needed to satisfy modeled safety and actuator constraints. A common implementation solves $\mathbf{u}^*=\arg\min_{\mathbf{u}}\|\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{u}_{\text{nom}}\|^2$ subject to barrier and input constraints, potentially acting before the safe-set boundary is reached. Its guarantee depends on feasibility, model and state bounds, and execution timing; minimizing input deviation neither maximizes task performance nor supplies a fallback when the feasible set is empty. (@Sec-enforcement, @sec-appendix-control-cbf)

**Mode Averaging (Multimodality Catastrophe)**
: A learning failure in which a regression policy averages distinct valid action modes into an unsuitable action, potentially causing a physical hazard. Mean squared error favors the conditional mean, which can lie between valid pathways. When human demonstrators navigate around an obstacle by choosing either a left or right detour, a naive regression model averages the competing action modes, commanding an interpolation that steers the robot directly into the obstacle. Mixture models, discrete strategy choices, or generative decoders can represent distinct modes; their selected actions still require physical feasibility checks. (@Sec-training, @sec-brain)

**Mode Confusion**
: A safety-critical cognitive misalignment between a human operator and an automated system regarding which entity possesses active control authority over specific physical degrees of freedom. Mode confusion arises when autonomous overrides engage or disengage silently without salient multisensory feedback, leading the human to believe they are steering while the autonomous policy is resisting, or vice versa. In safety-critical robotics, mode confusion can produce control conflicts, delayed takeover, or unintended disengagement of protective functions. (@Sec-intervention)

**Monitored Premise Expiration**
: The withdrawal of operational authority when runtime monitoring finds a required safety-case premise false or unknown, for example because measured temperature exceeds a limit or sensor packets are missing. Linking runtime telemetry to safety case warrants makes detectable premise failures grounds for restricting authority; unmonitored premises still require independent evidence. When a monitored premise expires, the system transitions autonomously into a restricted or refusal operational regime. (@Sec-release)

## O {#sec-glossary-vol4-o .unlisted}

**Observation Contract**
: A specification of the spatial, temporal, and semantic claims a perception subsystem supplies downstream, including coordinate frames, capture times, coverage, uncertainty, and validity flags. It distinguishes deterministic bounds from statistical confidence regions and names how detectable violations revoke a claim. A contract cannot make occluded or unmonitored conditions observable; unsupported claims must remain unknown. (@Sec-perception, @sec-brain)

**Observational Indistinguishability**
: A limitation in which distinct physical states requiring different responses produce the same available observation history up to the relevant intervention deadline. No algorithm using only that history can reliably distinguish the states in time. A conservative action valid in both states, independent evidence, or passive protection may still control the hazard; indistinguishability alone does not imply that all protective responses are impossible. (@Sec-frontier)

**Operational Design Domain (ODD)**
: The object poses, surface conditions, payloads, speeds, and disturbances in which a machine is meant to operate, written down as the scenario ledger. A dataset supports the part of the ODD that its occupancy join covers; the rest is its known absence. The sets nest: the policy manifest claims a declared ODD within the ODD, evaluation samples a target ODD within the declared ODD, and verification extends the target ODD to the machine's internal conditions as the operating envelope that a release verdict authorizes in whole, in part, or not at all. (@Sec-data-policy-coverage, @sec-training, @sec-evaluation, @sec-verification, @sec-release)

## P {#sec-glossary-vol4-p .unlisted}

**Physical Artificial Intelligence (Physical AI)**
: An interdisciplinary branch of artificial intelligence concerned with computational systems whose sensory inputs, inferential deliberations, and learning algorithms are intrinsically coupled to physical bodies operating within continuous, non-stationary physical environments. A physical AI system must reconcile inference latency with physical dynamical time scales, irreversible contact, and hardware constraints. Its engineering objective is useful closed-loop task execution within a supported operating and safety envelope. (@Sec-boundary, @sec-brain)

**Proposal Boundary**
: The line between a learned model, which may only propose an action, and the permission path, a mechanism designed to make the actuation decision independently of the model, within a qualified latency and fault envelope. The permission path checks each proposal against fresh evidence, the stopping envelope, and a fallback feasible from the current state, and it refuses when any check fails. The proposal boundary separates the Brain from the Nervous System in the book's five-level machine. (@Sec-boundary-machine-model, @sec-nervous, @sec-enforcement)

## Q {#sec-glossary-vol4-q .unlisted}

**Qualification Ladder (XIL)**
: A structured cyber-physical verification progression that systematically tests embodied AI systems across evaluation substrates of increasing physical and temporal realism: Model-in-the-Loop (MIL), Software-in-the-Loop (SIL), Processor-in-the-Loop (PIL), Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL), and In-Situ Physical Fault Injection. Because each stage closes or substitutes distinct physical and computational feedback loops, each rung exposes different integration effects; only the hardware and physical loops actually present can supply evidence about their contention, electrical transients, or actuator dynamics. The assurance argument selects complementary stages according to the claims and faults each can test. (@Sec-verification)

## R {#sec-glossary-vol4-r .unlisted}

**Record Chain**
: The fifteen records, one produced by each chapter of Parts I to IV except the one on the learned proposer and one by the conclusion, that carry the book's assumptions and evidence from the limit record to the residual-claims register. One strand states what the plant can do and what the proposer has shown it can do; the other carries what the proposer proposes now; they meet in the enforcement record. A record makes a claim inspectable; it does not establish the claim. (@Sec-boundary-book-architecture, @sec-appendix-systems-record-register)

## S {#sec-glossary-vol4-s .unlisted}

**Safe Torque Off (STO)**
: A drive safety function that prevents the drive from generating motor torque through its torque-producing power stage. STO does not itself brake a moving load, hold a gravity-loaded mechanism, or isolate the electrical supply. Its use in a stopping or restraint path requires a plant-specific assessment of coasting, stored energy, and any separately rated mechanical brake. (@Sec-enforcement, @sec-body)

**Safety Case (Claim–Argument–Evidence)**
: A structured, auditable assurance argument that demonstrates how an embodied AI system satisfies its explicit safety requirements within a declared operational design domain. It organizes assurance hierarchically by linking high-level claims to empirical and formal evidence (such as fault injection manifests, HIL qualification results, and barrier proofs) via transparent, falsifiable engineering arguments. In physical AI, the safety case explicitly binds software performance to physical hardware limits and operational envelopes. (@Sec-release)

**Shared Autonomy**
: A collaborative control architecture in which a human supervisor and an autonomous policy concurrently exert control authority over an embodied system's physical degrees of freedom. Authority allocation may be realized via continuous haptic virtual fixtures, dynamic compliance blending, or task-space privilege partitioning. The central challenge of shared autonomy is maintaining an intuitive, transparent authority distribution that avoids conflicting commands while preserving the qualified safety constraints. (@Sec-intervention)

**Sim-to-Real Contact Exploit**
: An optimization pathology wherein a reinforcement learning policy discovers and exploits unphysical numerical artifacts in a simulator's contact solver—such as interpenetration spring restitution, infinite friction sticking, or instantaneous impulse relaxation—to achieve high simulated reward. Because these mathematical solver relaxations do not exist in the physical world, the learned policy can lose performance or violate constraints when deployed on hardware. Mitigation can include improved contact models, randomized parameters, energy-consistency checks, and physical validation. (@Sec-training)

**Sim-to-Real Gap (Sim-to-Reality Gap)**
: The systematic discrepancy in dynamics, contact mechanics, sensor transduction, and execution latency that exists between a computational physics simulation and the real physical environment. Policies optimized purely in simulation frequently fail upon physical deployment when the selected models omit or misrepresent effects such as frictional contact, transmission backlash, compliance, or execution delay. Bridging this gap is the central challenge of simulation-based policy training in physical AI. (@Sec-training, @sec-evaluation)

**Spatial Information Age ($t_{\text{age}}$)**
: The total wall-clock elapsed time between the physical capture epoch of a sensor observation and the exact moment that observation is utilized to make an actuation decision: $t_{\text{age}} = t_{\text{act}} - t_{\text{capture}}$. In dynamic environments, a speed bound $v_{\text{max}}$ yields a possible displacement $v_{\text{max}}t_{\text{age}}$ during that interval, which must be reflected in the uncertainty or clearance model. State estimation pipelines must enforce explicit information-age bounds to prevent policies from acting on stale world representations. (@Sec-perception, @sec-memory)

**Stopping Suffix**
: A precomputed braking trajectory reserved with an admitted motion plan to reach a controlled standstill within declared clearance and actuator limits. It is usable only from its validated entry region, with the necessary state continuity, traction, drive authority, and power available. If authority expires from another state, the permission path needs a separately qualified state-matched response. (@Sec-planning, @sec-intervention)

## T {#sec-glossary-vol4-t .unlisted}

**Takeover Reaction Budget ($T_{\Sigma}$)**
: The supervisory waiting interval from a takeover demand to receipt of the first human command, modeled here as $T_{\Sigma}=T_{\text{sensory}}+T_{\text{cognitive}}+T_{\text{motor}}+T_{\text{comm}}$. The communication term includes transport and the authority handshake; plant response, braking, and any subsequent blending require separate budget terms. A takeover can be credited with preventing harm only if this complete response fits before the last feasible intervention time. (@Sec-intervention)

**Temporal Ensembling**
: A filtering technique for action-chunked policies that combines predictions for the same execution time from overlapping chunks, often through an exponentially weighted average. It can reduce inter-chunk discontinuities but does not guarantee bounded jerk, preserve distinct action modes, or establish feasibility. Weighting older predictions also trades responsiveness for smoothing. (@Sec-brain, @sec-training, @sec-planning)

**Time-to-Harm ($t_{\text{harm}}$)**
: The predicted interval until a specified harmful event under a stated continuation of the current motion and disturbance assumptions. Comparing it with detection, decision, actuation, and braking time helps assess response urgency, but a scalar timing inequality alone does not prove clearance or forward invariance. A protective response must begin while it remains feasible; once that region is lost, initiating emergency braking cannot guarantee avoidance. (@Sec-frontier)

**Trajectory Spline Blending ($C^2$ Continuity)**
: Interpolation across trajectory seams that matches position, velocity, and acceleration through $C^2$ continuity, using suitably constrained polynomials or splines. Acceleration continuity removes acceleration steps but does not imply continuous jerk, which requires $C^3$ continuity, or bound the magnitude of jerk. The blend must separately satisfy velocity, acceleration, jerk, torque, and clearance limits over the entire segment. (@Sec-planning, @sec-brain)

## V {#sec-glossary-vol4-v .unlisted}

**Vision-Language-Action (VLA) Model**
: A multimodal model that conditions action predictions on visual observations and language, often with robot proprioception. Outputs may be discrete action tokens, continuous controls, or trajectory chunks. Built on high-capacity transformer backbones pretrained on Internet-scale vision-language datasets and fine-tuned on robotics demonstrations, VLA models synthesize open-vocabulary semantic reasoning with spatial affordance grounding. Because their internal weights lack physical safety and stability guarantees, their outputs are treated as unprivileged candidate proposals requiring downstream kinodynamic and barrier filtering. (@Sec-brain, @sec-intent)

## W {#sec-glossary-vol4-w .unlisted}

**World Model**
: An internal generative model that learns to simulate the forward transition dynamics, contact mechanics, and sensory observations of the physical environment conditioned on the agent's prospective actions. In physical AI, world models support counterfactual trajectory evaluation and model-predictive rollouts without executing each candidate on hardware. A learned predictive model is not automatically a validated digital twin. Their reliability is fundamentally constrained by epistemic uncertainty over non-smooth contact bifurcations and the sim-to-real reality gap. (@Sec-brain, @sec-planning, @sec-training)

\normalsize
```
